extracted.intended_audience: Researchers and PIs applying to NIH (including early-stage investigators) seeking practical guidance on application submission, review, and funding outcomes
extracted.subtask_description: Practical Q&A guidance on NIH grant submission, review scores/percentiles, programmatic funding decisions, JIT/administrative processing, resubmission strategy, and budget/other-support issues for NIH mechanisms (R01, R03, R21, R35, K, U01, DP2, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Final funding decisions prioritize scientific merit and programmatic priority
rubrics_metrics.description: The final decision is not made on whether someone has money or not – many factors are taken into consideration, starting with scientific merit and programmatic priority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Having other funding is not a disqualifier and PIs can hold multiple awards (even 2 R01s). Program officers will weigh scientific merit and IC priorities; funding status may be one consideration among many (e.g., to avoid forcing a lab to close), but not the determinative factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Payline and percentile determine fundability
rubrics_metrics.description: The payline is what matters, and these are usually based on percentiles, so your percentile needs to be at or below the payline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check the IC's payline and use percentiles to interpret fundability; contact PO for advice if percentile is above payline. Percentiles are often used as basis for awarding but may be flexible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scores in the 'grey zone' have uncertain funding probability
rubrics_metrics.description: Scores around ~30 can be in a 'grey zone' where funding probability is uncertain (some in the low 30s have been funded historically).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect uncertainty — POs may estimate probabilities (e.g., 80% chance) and decisions depend on skips, appropriation, and programmatic needs. Consider whether to prepare backup applications rather than rely solely on grey-zone chances.

rubrics_metrics.name: A1 resubmission does not automatically harm A0 funding
rubrics_metrics.description: An A0 can still be funded even if an A1 is submitted and receives a different score; an A1 score does not necessarily determine the A0 outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdotal experience shows A0s have been funded after A1 was not discussed. Applicants sometimes submit an A1 'for insurance' but later withdraw if not needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notices of Special Interest (NOSIs) can provide programmatic advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: NOSIs reflect where ICs are investing for programmatic priority and demonstrate an investigator’s interest in an IC’s special interests; instructions/review criteria can differ from standard PAs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PIs should pay attention to NOSIs and apply if appropriate; NOSI respondents may get extra funding consideration (ICs may make extra awards in that area). NOSIs will gradually replace some PAs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Just-In-Time (JIT) requests indicate impending processing — be prepared
rubrics_metrics.description: Your status will change when the GMS or PO requests your JIT; they will contact you when your application is next in line for processing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have all documentation (Other Support, IRB/IACUC, budgets, institutional approvals) ready because JIT turnarounds can be very short (a day or two). If you cannot respond quickly, IC may move to next application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report overlaps on the Other Support/Support Form
rubrics_metrics.description: You want to report overlaps, whether it’s a subaim or a whole application. NIH needs to ensure you are not being funded for the same work twice and that you have the effort to commit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report pending and active support. If both applications are funded, be ready to adjust the later award to eliminate overlap. Be transparent — GMS will find out eventually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect costs for subawards are part of the grant's direct costs
rubrics_metrics.description: The indirect costs of a subaward are part of the Direct costs of the grant. A 25% subaward refers to total costs (direct plus indirect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When budgeting, determine how much you need to send the subawardee to get the work done, then add their indirect costs; institutional grants office can provide exact calculations and templates.

rubrics_metrics.name: No strict time limit to renew an R01 but science must remain relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no time limit on the gap between the conclusion of a Type 1 R01 and submission of the Type 2 renewal, but the science must still be relevant to the original project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check FOA for whether renewals are accepted and weigh budget caps vs. submitting a new Type 1. Long gaps may make renewal less appropriate if the premise has changed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing renewals to avoid funding lapses
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim to have the renewal start in the same fiscal year that the current grant ends to minimize lapses in funding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan submission dates (e.g., Feb/March for FY alignment) so that review/council timing allows a renewal start that matches your current end date; consider institutional cushion/carryover or NCE.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consultants vs co-investigators/co-PIs when proposing unfamiliar techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: If proposing techniques you have no direct hands-on experience with, reviewers will be concerned; having consultants write support letters is less convincing than including them as co-investigators who will perform the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For central methods, make key collaborators co-investigators or co-PIs (balance with ESI status concerns). R01 is not a mentored mechanism — don't use it for on-the-job training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of letters of support is not inherently negative
rubrics_metrics.description: More letters of support (e.g., 3-4) do not generally look bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For ESIs include an institutional support letter (department chair or director) confirming commitment to PI's development, space, resources, and mentoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Percentiles may be absent or misleading for some mechanisms/FOAs
rubrics_metrics.description: Some FOAs (e.g., many R03s) are targeted and don't have enough submissions to permit percentiling, so percentiles may be omitted or misleading (percentiles are calculated against study section submissions over the last 3 rounds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret scores and percentiles with caution; scores can provide more flexibility than percentiles for funding decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: No rule prohibits recycling text, but update and justify reused material
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no NIH rule preventing you from submitting identical text again, but recycled text may be problematic if it makes your submission appear stale or unproductive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Update Significance/Aims/Background to reflect new data and current state of the science; for renewal applications, use prior accomplishments to motivate new aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Being on the paylist does not guarantee an award — position matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Being on the paylist is positive but not a guarantee; paylists often contain more applications than funds allow, so where you sit on the list matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If PO explicitly indicates your app 'should be on our paylist to be funded' and gives strong wording, funding is likely but NOA is the definitive proof. Administrative steps (GMS, IC Director) still needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deferred funding decisions can be carried through the fiscal year
rubrics_metrics.description: Deferred funding decisions are made through the end of the fiscal year (September); an application can remain capable of being funded until administratively removed (often a couple of years), though funding in a subsequent FY is rare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that some applications may be held for later consideration; lack of immediate NOA doesn't mean permanent rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contacting PO: wait until appropriate status changes or PO outreach
rubrics_metrics.description: You don’t need to contact the PO about status while waiting for JIT; they will contact you when appropriate. If your percentile is above payline, contacting PO for next-step advice is reasonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you have not heard after council and no JIT, you can check with PO for advice on resubmission, rebuttal, or other steps — but don’t expect additional information until processing begins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changing role to MPI/co-PI after review likely requires new review
rubrics_metrics.description: Changing from co-I to MPI/co-PI is considered a significant change and will likely require new review because it changes leadership and management plans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you need MPI status, consider changing on an A1 or wait until renewal or after first RPPR to demonstrate MPI-level contributions; discuss with PO for best timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple awards and concurrent funding considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: PIs can have multiple awards; ICs sometimes prefer funding applicants without concurrent funding if choosing among similarly scored applications to preserve labs at risk of closure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you already have significant funding (e.g., R00), this may factor into programmatic decisions, but it is not an automatic disqualifier. Speak with PO for candid guidance on priorities and likelihood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resubmission rules vary by mechanism — R03/R21 specifics
rubrics_metrics.description: For some mechanisms (e.g., R03), if the FOA is still active you can submit again as a new A0 even after an A1; you should not include an Introduction/rebuttal referencing the A1 but should revise per critiques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether to change title if the emphasis or data change; check FOA for resubmission policies and consult PO if unsure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funded probability is affected by 'skips' (applicants withdrawing due to other awards)
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of 'skips' at lower scores (because applicants accept other awards) can shift funding outcomes, enabling higher-scored applications to be funded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical funding trends and RePORT data can help estimate outcomes; expect variability year-to-year depending on number of applications/appropriations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use NIH RePORT and Reporter tools to check institute funding trends
rubrics_metrics.description: NIGMS and other ICs publish funding trends (applications/awards by percentile) on RePORT; use Reporter advanced search to see funded apps by FY, activity code, and IC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check https://report.nih.gov/nihdatabook and https://reporter.nih.gov/advanced-search to evaluate past funding behavior for your activity code and IC.

rubrics_metrics.name: JIT-to-NOA timing can vary; Cycle III awards typically issued in July
rubrics_metrics.description: After JIT, several weeks or months can pass before status changes and NOA issuance; Cycle III awards are often issued in July and awards may continue through September.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be patient and keep institutional compliance ready. If JIT is requested, respond quickly to avoid being bypassed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose pending non-NIH funding that overlaps; non-overlapping industry contracts generally ok
rubrics_metrics.description: NIH wants to know about overlap; other active support such as large contracts for non-overlapping projects typically do not affect R21/R01 approval unless there is overlap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document overlaps clearly and be prepared to adjust scope if dual funding occurs. Institutional grants office can advise on specific cases.
